newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel capital market reforms face opposition.
newsitem.headline: Israel capital market reforms face opposition.

text.p: An Israeli government-appointed committee proposed sweeping measures on Tuesday to revive the country's ailing capital markets but the reforms faced numerous critics, which even included the central bank.

The proposals want to cut dividend tax on publicly traded firms to 15 from 25 percent, create a secondary mortgage market, allow the Bank of Israel to operate in the money market, reform pensions and impose new taxes on savings.

"We thought this was the proper way to resuscitate the capital markets," committee chairman David Brodett, who is also director-general of the Finance Ministry, told a news conference to announce the committee's findings.

The proposals, many of which could go into effect in 1997, will be presented to the government for approval. All tax changes require parliamentary legislation and some analysts predicted that several measures would not be approved.
"The direction is right but implementation will be difficult," said Doron Tsur, head of research at Sahar Securities.
The most controversial proposals concern pension fund reform and new taxes on savings of less than 10 years.
Zvi Hoffman of Meitav Investments doubted a tax on short-term savings would pass. "Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu promised he would not do anything to harm savers."
The central bank issued a statement stressing the importance of stimulating savings at a time when savings both in the public and private sector have been declining.

Finance Minister Dan Meridor called for the creation of the committee in July, as stock and bond prices were plunging amid investor flight from provident funds, a popular long-term investment instrument in Israel.
High interest rates aimed at fighting rising inflation have enticed investors away from provident funds and into high-yielding, shorter-term savings accounts.
"It is not currently desirable to impose a new tax on savings of different durations," the central bank said.
The Histadrut labour federation warned it would fight any attempt to change the pension agreement with the government.
The committee proposes encouraging workers to save more in pension funds by raising the amount of their wages eligible for tax benefits.
At the same time pension funds would be allowed to invest less in special high-yielding bonds the government issues for pension funds.
The committee believes pension funds will then invest more in other securities, estimating this change would bring 10 billion shekels to the capital markets by 2010.
But the Histadrut fears this will erode the returns on pension savings. "We oppose the recommendations that change the pension fund agreements," Histadrut leader Amir Peretz said on Israel Radio.
The committee recommends the changes take effect in 1997 but several will include a three-year transition phase.

"It is unfortunate the recommendations address only the long term and provide no solution to what must happen tomorrow morning," said Danny Gillerman, president of the Federation of Israel Chambers of Commerce.

Prime Minister Netanyahu of the Likud party took office three months ago saying his programme of structural reforms, deregulation and privatisation would open the economy to competition and remove the socialist vestiges of the previous Labour party government.
($1=3.17 shekels)
